stops.name: Buenos Aires, Un cuarto propio in Spanish
stops.campa: Editorial Sur brings out A Room of One's Own as Un cuarto propio, the translation credited to Leonor Acevedo de Borges, mother of Jorge Luis, though the collaboration between mother and son on so exact a feminist text is generally understood to run deeper than the credit line. Victoria's reading of Woolf's essay, only two years before she founded Sur, had already fed directly into her own sense that a woman needed an income and a room of her own to write in; publishing it in Spanish is, for her, less a business decision than a repayment of a debt.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Teatro Colón, dancing Perséphone
stops.campa: Introduced to Igor Stravinsky in Paris in 1932 by the conductor Ernst Ansermet, Victoria brings the composer and his son Soulima to stay and rehearse at her own house before the Teatro Colón premiere of his melodrama Perséphone; on the night itself she herself takes the speaking role of Persephone, the one moment in her life the forbidden vocation of the stage is publicly permitted her. Afterward Stravinsky gives her the manuscript with a dedication of gratitude. She will call the whole episode, decades later, the most painfully happy memory of her life, painful because she was never again allowed to do the thing she did best.
stops.quote: Perséfone es el recuerdo más dolorosamente feliz de mi vida. Digo dolorosamente porque me hubiera gustado seguir haciendo ese tipo de cosas, que es lo que mejor he hecho en mi vida.
stops.quote_source: Late-life reminiscence, quoted in Radio Perfil, '7 de abril de 1890 nació Victoria Ocampo'

stops.name: London, the break with Virginia Woolf
stops.campa: On what proves to be their last meeting, Victoria, wanting a record of the friendship, arranges for the German photographer Gisèle Freund to photograph Woolf without adequately warning her; Woolf, who detests being photographed and feels ambushed, is deeply offended, and the friendship that had run since 1934 through devoted letters effectively ends here, months before the war that will kill Woolf by her own hand two years later. Victoria will go on publishing her in Spanish for another three decades regardless, the debt of the reader outlasting the wound of the friend.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, editing Les Lettres Françaises in exile
stops.campa: With occupied France silenced, Victoria and her collaborator Pelegrina Pastorino found and edit, from neutral Buenos Aires, a magazine called Les Lettres Françaises, gathering the work of French writers who cannot publish under Vichy or the German occupation and circulating it back across the Atlantic wherever it can reach. It is an act of considerable personal risk and expense in a country whose government leans toward the Axis, and it fixes her, for the wartime years, as the most visible anti-fascist voice of Argentine letters, the role Sur's 1937 declaration had already prepared her for.

stops.name: Nuremberg, the sole Argentine at the trials
stops.campa: Victoria travels to occupied Germany to attend, as the only Argentine present, sessions of the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, where the surviving leadership of the Nazi state is tried before the world. She sits through testimony of the camps and the machinery of extermination with the same exactness she has brought to every text she has ever edited, understanding the tribunal itself as a document her generation is obliged to witness in person rather than read about; the experience will feed her postwar writing on freedom, justice, and the fragility of civilization for the rest of her life.

stops.name: New York, meeting Albert Camus
stops.campa: In New York, where Camus is touring after the war and Victoria has already translated his Caligula for Sur, the two meet in person for the first time. What begins is a friendship that will run until his death in 1960, fed by fourteen years of correspondence marked, on his side, by teasing complaints about her telephone manners and, on both sides, by an unshakeable common commitment to intellectual freedom against every totalitarianism, of the right or the left, that the mid-century throws up. He will visit her at Villa Ocampo; she will visit him in Paris; the friendship survives illness, distance, and, later, her own imprisonment.
stops.quote: Su teléfono es tan sordo como Dios Padre. (Your telephone is as deaf as God the Father.)
stops.quote_source: Camus to Ocampo, Victoria Ocampo & Albert Camus, Correspondencia (1946-1959)

stops.name: Mar del Plata, arrest at her own seaside house
stops.campa: Weeks after two bombs kill several people at a Peronist rally in the Plaza de Mayo, the government of Juan Domingo Perón, hunting for instigators among its known opponents, arrests Victoria at her house in Mar del Plata. She has never hidden her contempt for the regime; Sur has never printed a line in its favor; the accusation of complicity in a bombing is transparently a pretext to silence the country's most visible anti-Peronist woman of letters. She is sixty-three years old and is taken from the seaside house directly into custody.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El Buen Pastor, twenty-six days among the condemned
stops.campa: Victoria is transferred to the women's prison of El Buen Pastor in San Telmo, a colonial building once a Jesuit retreat house and, since 1890, a penitentiary run by nuns for the correction of women deemed of ill repute: prostitutes, thieves, the destitute. Here the founder of Sur, the friend of Ortega and Woolf and Tagore, shares a cell block and a routine with the poorest women of her own city, an inversion so complete it becomes, in the telling afterward, the emblem of the whole Peronist decade's assault on the old liberal elite she embodies.

stops.name: Paris, Camus and the writers' committee
stops.campa: Word of the arrest crosses the Atlantic within days. Albert Camus, who has stayed at Villa Ocampo, personally drafts a letter of protest and delivers it to the Argentine ambassador in Paris; Aldous Huxley and Waldo Frank organize a committee demanding the release of all writers unjustly imprisoned in Argentina; Gabriela Mistral cables Perón directly; Jawaharlal Nehru, prime minister of India, adds his own pressure through diplomatic channels that trace straight back to the friendship begun with Tagore thirty years before. The cell in San Telmo becomes, briefly, a fact of international literary politics.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, released, under surveillance
stops.campa: After twenty-six days Victoria is released without trial, the charges never substantiated, but she remains under close police surveillance for the two years that remain of Perón's government, until his fall in September 1955. Two weeks after her release she writes to the international writers who campaigned for her, describing the imprisonment plainly, without self-pity, as a fact to be recorded rather than mourned; the letter becomes, in later scholarship, one of the few first-person testimonies of Peronist-era political imprisonment written by a woman of her class and stature.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, honorary doctorate from Visva-Bharati
stops.campa: On a state visit to Argentina, Indira Gandhi, prime minister of India and, since her father's death, chancellor of the university Tagore founded at Santiniketan, confers on Victoria an honorary degree from Visva-Bharati in the name of the institution named for the poet who once called her Vijaya. Forty-four years after the convalescence at Villa Miralrío, India returns to close the circle formally: the private devotion of 1924 is folded into a public honor passed from one generation of the Nehru-Gandhi line to another, from the Mahatma's admirer to the daughter of the man who once helped free her from a Peronist cell.

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo given to UNESCO
stops.campa: At eighty-three, Victoria formally donates the house her father built in Beccar, the house where Tagore convalesced and Stravinsky rehearsed, to UNESCO, ensuring it will outlive her as a place of cultural exchange rather than pass into private hands or be broken up among heirs. The gift is entirely in character: everything she has built across five decades, the magazine, the publishing house, the friendships spanning four continents, was always meant to serve a circulation of ideas larger than her own name; the house is simply the last and largest object she has to give to that circulation.
